Create a latent factor specification

Source: R/latent.R
latent_factor.Rd

Define latent factors for unmeasured structure shared by the responses of a model. A unit l carries scores \(u_{l f} \sim N(0, 1)\) on factors \(f = 1, \ldots, K\), and response s loads on them with loadings \(\lambda_{s f}\), so its linear predictor gains \(\sum_f \lambda_{s f} u_{l f}\). The factors add the covariance \(\Lambda \Lambda^\top\) between the linear predictors of the responses of one unit.

Usage

latent_factor(
  n_factors = 1L,
  unit = NULL,
  response = NULL,
  prior = NULL,
  shared = TRUE,
  constraint = NULL
)

# S3 method for class 'tulpa_latent'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

n_factors

Integer; number of latent factors. Default is 1.

unit

For tulpa()'s factors = argument: the name of the column of data holding the unit that carries the scores (e.g. "site").

response

For tulpa()'s factors = argument: the name of the column of data holding the response level each row belongs to (e.g. "species"). Each level has its own fixed effects and loadings.

prior

Prior of the factor loadings, or NULL for the fitter's default. tulpa() carries a normal prior centred at zero on every loading, folded onto the positive half-line on the diagonal, and takes prior_normal(0, sd) (default sd = 1); a model package may read other priors (tulpaRatio defaults to a PC prior with P(loading > 1) = 0.01 on the diagonal loadings).

shared

Logical; if TRUE (default), the factors load on every process of the model. If FALSE, they load on the first process only (a two-process model package's numerator); tulpa() requires TRUE.

constraint

NULL (default) or the identifiability constraint a sampling fitter pins the scores with: "sum_to_zero" (each factor's scores sum to zero across units) or "first_zero" (the first unit's scores are zero). tulpa() requires NULL: its scores carry a proper N(0, 1) prior and each response's intercept absorbs their level.

x

A tulpa_latent specification.

...

Ignored.

Value

A tulpa_latent object.

Details

Identification

The product \(\lambda_{s f} u_{l f}\) is unchanged by a rescaling, a sign flip and, for several factors, a rotation of the scores against the loadings. The unit variance of the scores fixes the scale; a loading matrix that is lower-triangular with a positive diagonal fixes the sign and the rotation. \(\Lambda \Lambda^\top\) is invariant to all three, so it is the quantity to compare across fits.

Choosing n_factors

With S responses, \(\Lambda\) lower-triangular has \(S K - K (K - 1) / 2\) free loadings against the \(S (S + 1) / 2\) entries of a covariance between the responses, so at most S factors fit. A two-process model is full rank at n_factors = 2.

Relationship to Random Effects

A random intercept is one response's deviation per group; a factor is a deviation per unit that every response reads with its own loading, so it carries the residual correlation between responses that the covariates do not explain.

See also

tulpa() (factors =), latent_factors() for the scores, prior_normal()

Examples

# Two factors over sites, one response level per species
latent_factor(n_factors = 2, unit = "site", response = "species")
#> Latent factor specification
#> ===========================
#> 
#> Number of factors: 2 
#> Unit column: site 
#> Response column: species 
#> Shared: Yes (loads on all processes) 
#> Constraint: none (proper score prior) 
#> 
#> Loading prior:
#>   the fitter's default

# A tighter loading prior
latent_factor(unit = "site", response = "species",
              prior = prior_normal(0, 0.5))
#> Latent factor specification
#> ===========================
#> 
#> Number of factors: 1 
#> Unit column: site 
#> Response column: species 
#> Shared: Yes (loads on all processes) 
#> Constraint: none (proper score prior) 
#> 
#> Loading prior:
#>   Normal(0.00, 0.50)

# \donttest{
set.seed(1)
n_site <- 60; n_sp <- 4
u <- rnorm(n_site)
lambda <- c(0.8, 0.5, -0.6, 0.3)
d <- expand.grid(site = factor(seq_len(n_site)),
                 species = factor(paste0("sp", seq_len(n_sp))))
d$x <- rnorm(n_site)[d$site]
d$y <- rpois(nrow(d), exp(0.5 + 0.3 * d$x +
                          lambda[d$species] * u[d$site]))
fit <- tulpa(y ~ x, data = d, family = "poisson",
             factors = latent_factor(unit = "site", response = "species"))
fit$loadings
#>        factor1
#> sp1  0.7542586
#> sp2  0.3246828
#> sp3 -0.4679399
#> sp4  0.1682484
# }
